The Culture of Accountability in Islamic Parties, Organisations, and Institutions: The Hefazat Ameer’s Recent Controversial Remarks and the Tendency to Defend Rather Than Accept Accountability

Accountability is one of the fundamental prerequisites for transparency, ethical discipline, and healthy development in every sphere—whether at the individual, organisational, political, or institutional level. The institutional capacity and public credibility of any organisation depend not merely on its declared ideals, programmes, or achievements, but also, to a considerable extent, on how transparent, refined, responsible, and accountable the conduct of its leadership is.

The practice of accountability is particularly important for organisations and institutions that claim to represent Islamic ideals, ethics, and values. This is because their organisational conduct and the ethical standing of their leadership influence not only the public image of the organisations themselves but also, in many cases, public perceptions of Islamic ideals and Islamic institutions as a whole.

Regrettably, however, this culture of accountability has not become sufficiently institutionalised in many of our Islamic parties, organisations, and institutions. In particular, the organisational and administrative structures of many Qawmi educational institutions have long exhibited a tendency towards the absolute authority of institutional heads and personality-centred leadership.

In many cases, the head of an institution is effectively regarded as the ultimate authority, while no effective and independent institutional mechanism exists to review or question their decisions and activities. Even where governing bodies or Shura councils exist, questions remain as to whether they are actually functioning as effective accountability mechanisms in every case.

Consequently, instead of ensuring accountability in leadership, an individual's personal status and authority often become the principal determinants of organisational management.

The same tendency can also be observed in some Islamic parties and organisations. Senior leaders and heads of institutions are, in practice, often treated as being above accountability. When errors, shortcomings, or ethical lapses are identified in their statements, decisions, or conduct, there is often a tendency to justify and defend them through various explanations, arguments, and rationalisations rather than undertake an impartial review and initiate corrective measures. Sometimes, criticism is sidestepped in the name of personal loyalty, sometimes in the name of organisational interests, and sometimes under the pretext of protecting the institution's public image.

Yet an individual's mistakes do not automatically become the responsibility of the entire organisation. However, when an organisation institutionally engages in defending such mistakes instead of properly evaluating and correcting them, the individual's controversial conduct gradually becomes an organisational liability.

As a result, the very effort to conceal mistakes in order to protect the organisation's reputation may ultimately call into question its overall credibility and legacy.

It is important to remember that protecting the reputation of a party, organisation, or institution is more important than protecting the reputation of an individual; and safeguarding the integrity of truth and principle is far more important than protecting the reputation of any party, organisation, or institution.

Just as it is inappropriate to impose the responsibility for an individual's mistakes or controversial conduct upon an entire organisation, it is equally unacceptable to undermine the dignity of its underlying ideals under the pretext of protecting the organisation's public image.

In reality, however, individuals are sometimes protected at the cost of exposing their organisations to public criticism; conversely, organisations are sometimes defended in ways that bring the very ideals they claim to uphold into controversy. Such tendencies can hardly be regarded as signs of prudent organisational conduct.

Rather, in order to preserve the reputation and credibility of their ideals, the leadership of organisations and institutions must be subject to effective accountability. Impartial reviews of leadership errors and irregularities, necessary corrective measures, appropriate disciplinary action, and, in serious cases, removal from office should all be regarded as normal components of healthy organisational management.

Accountability does not necessarily mean punishing someone. Rather, it is an institutional process that involves seeking explanations for mistakes, verifying the facts, acknowledging errors, making corrections, and taking appropriate measures where necessary. Regrettably, however, there are relatively few visible examples of such effective accountability mechanisms being established in many of our Islamic organisations and institutions.

Hefazat-e-Islam is one of the country's large and influential organisations within the Islamic sphere. Its Ameer is also an elderly religious figure, whose age and standing deserve due respect. However, a person's age, status, or organisational position cannot place them above accountability. The controversy that has emerged recently over some of his statements and the language used in them provides a relevant example in this regard.

In response to such statements, one would have expected the organisation first to undertake an impartial internal review and, where necessary, bring the relevant leadership under appropriate accountability mechanisms. This would have made it possible, on the one hand, to preserve the personal dignity of the leader and, on the other, to safeguard the organisation's ethical standing and institutional credibility.

When, instead, there is a repeated tendency to offer explanations and defences in support of the statements, the controversy ceases to remain confined to the words of the individual concerned. The entire organisation is then drawn into public criticism and scrutiny. In this way, the organisation itself narrows the very space that could have allowed it to distinguish its institutional identity from the responsibility for an individual's statements.

It is important to remember that showing respect to an Ameer or leader, or demonstrating loyalty to an organisation, does not mean endorsing every statement or action of that individual. Rather, genuine organisational loyalty is demonstrated by identifying mistakes as mistakes, allowing leadership the opportunity to correct them, and ensuring accountability when necessary. Accepting criticism not as hostility but as an essential part of self-reflection and institutional excellence is the hallmark of a healthy organisational culture.

People expect Islamic organisations not merely to propagate Islamic ideals, but also to demonstrate in their own organisational lives the practical application of justice, trustworthiness, civility, Shura, transparency, and accountability. If these values are absent from their organisational practices while they continue to claim ideological superiority, the result will ultimately be a crisis of credibility.

It is essential not only to speak in defence of Islamic ideals but also to ensure that those ideals are reflected in leadership conduct and organisational management. After all, the superiority of an ideal is established not merely through words, but also through the conduct of its adherents and the institutional practices they uphold.
